```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(funresMech)
```

## What the package does

A functional response experiment exposes one consumer (a parasitoid or a
predator) to a known number of hosts or prey for a fixed time and records how
many were parasitized or consumed. funresMech fits a *mechanistic* model to
these counts: instead of assuming that the counts follow a binomial or
beta-binomial distribution, it simulates the foraging process (searching,
encountering and handling hosts) many times and uses the simulated
frequencies as the probability of each possible count (Okuyama 2012, 2026).
The parameters are then estimated by maximum likelihood.

The model has five parameters:

| Parameter | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `a` | Encounter-rate coefficient. The encounter rate at density *x* is a *x*^*z*. |
| `z` | Density-scaling exponent. *z* = 1 gives a type II response and *z* > 1 a type III (sigmoid) response. |
| `h` | Mean handling time, in the time unit of the experiment. |
| `k` | Regularity of search times: their squared coefficient of variation is 1/*k*. Small *k* means very irregular search. |
| `s` | Standard deviation of handling times. `s = 0` means a fixed handling time. |

The main question is usually the value of *z*, so *z* is estimated by
likelihood profiling: it is fixed at each value of a grid, the other
parameters are optimized, and the 95% interval contains the values of *z*
whose negative log-likelihood (NLL) is at most 1.92 units above the minimum.

## The data

One row per trial, with the host (or prey) density and the number of hosts
parasitized (or prey consumed). The default column names are `dens` and
`par`; other names are given with the arguments `dens` and `response`.

```{r data}
d <- data.frame(
  dens = rep(c(2, 5, 10, 20, 40), each = 6),
  par  = c(1, 2, 1, 2, 2, 1,  4, 3, 4, 5, 4, 3,  7, 8, 6, 8, 7, 9,
           11, 12, 13, 10, 12, 11,  16, 15, 17, 14, 16, 18)
)
head(d)
```

## Step 1: screen the data

Some trials can be very unlikely under the rest of the data, for example a
trial in which a parasitoid attacked almost nothing at a density where all
other parasitoids attacked most hosts. Such a trial can dominate the fit.
`screen_outliers()` flags these trials in a few seconds. It never removes
them: check flagged trials in the original records and, if they are kept,
report the analysis with and without them.

```{r screen}
scr <- screen_outliers(d, T = 24)
scr[scr$flagged, ]
```

## Step 2: specify the model

`funres_model()` defines the foraging process. The default has Gamma search
times, lognormal handling times and the parasitoid process (attacked hosts
remain available and can be found again).

```{r model}
funres_model()
```

Other choices are described in
`vignette("process-and-distributions", package = "funresMech")`.

## Step 3: fit

`fit_funres()` needs the data, the trial duration `T` and, optionally, the
model and the settings. The settings are chosen with a preset of
`funres_control()`:

* `"exploratory"`: a quick first look. **Not for reporting.**
* `"standard"` (default): for results to be reported, after verification.
* `"final"`: the highest precision.

```{r presets}
funres_control("standard")
```

The likelihood is approximated by simulation, so a fit takes from minutes to
hours. Evaluate the profile in parallel to save time:

```{r fit, eval = FALSE}
future::plan(future::multisession)       # use the available processor cores
set.seed(1)                              # results are reproducible with the seed
fit <- fit_funres(d, T = 24, time_unit = "h",
                  control = funres_control("standard"))
fit
```

The printed fit shows the estimates with their units, the 95% interval of
*z*, the AIC comparison with *z* = 1 and with a beta-binomial model, and a
summary of the reliability checks. This is the output of an exploratory fit
of a real dataset (64 trials, 13 densities):

```
Mechanistic functional response model (simulation-based likelihood)
  Process:        parasitoid (hosts not removed; distinct hosts counted)
  Search times:   gamma, mean 1/(a x^z), CV^2 = 1/k
  Handling times: lognormal, mean h, SD s
  Free parameters: a, h, z, k, s

Estimates (T = 24 h; 64 trials):
  a  = 0.01439      encounter-rate coefficient (1/h per host^2)
  h  = 0.5912       mean handling time (h)
  z  = 2            density-scaling exponent
  k  = 0.0172       search dispersion (CV^2 = 1/k)
  s  = 0.3452       SD of handling time (h)
  95% interval of z: [1.64, open]

Reliability: WARNING (cheap checks only; run verify_fit() before reporting).
 * [warning] Monte Carlo noise of the NLL: SE of the NLL at the optimum = 0.505
 * [warning] Interval of z closed: open upper limit
 * [warning] Search dispersion k not extreme: k = 0.0172
 * [warning] Settings suitable for reporting: exploratory preset
```

Here the warnings say what to do next: refit with the standard preset (less
Monte Carlo noise) and look at the open upper limit of *z*, which goes
together with a very small *k*.

## Step 4: verify before reporting

`verify_fit()` refits the model at the estimate of *z* in independent runs,
with more effort and with wider search bounds. `reliability()` then lists
every check with its status and the recommended action.

```{r verify, eval = FALSE}
fit <- verify_fit(fit)
reliability(fit)
```

Report a fit only when no check fails, and act on the warnings. See
`vignette("reliability", package = "funresMech")`.

## Step 5: use the fit

```{r use, eval = FALSE}
coef(fit)                 # estimates
fit$ci                    # interval of z
fit$profile               # likelihood profile of z
fit$aic                   # comparison with z = 1 and with the beta-binomial model

# Simulated experiments under the fitted model, for example to compare their
# distribution with the data or to plan a new experiment
sims <- simulate_response(fit$model, dens = c(2, 10, 40), T = 24,
                          par = coef(fit), n_sim = 1000)
```

`simulate_response()` can also be used before an experiment to see which
designs can distinguish type II from type III responses:

```{r simulate}
set.seed(1)
sims <- simulate_response(dens = c(2, 10, 40), T = 24,
                          par = c(a = 0.012, h = 0.6, z = 2.5, k = 0.9, s = 0.5),
                          n_sim = 200)
tapply(sims$response, sims$dens, mean)
```

## The interactive application

Every step above is available without writing code:

```{r app, eval = FALSE}
run_app()
```

The application reads a CSV file, lets you choose the columns, the time
unit, the model and the preset, runs the fit and the verification, and
exports the results, an R script that repeats the analysis and an HTML
report.

## References

Okuyama T (2012). A likelihood approach for functional response models.
*Biological Control* 60: 103–107.

Okuyama T (2026). Parametric assumptions in parasitoid functional response
analysis. *Journal of Applied Entomology*.
